# Bug Catalog: `verify/grapple_intercept.gd`

**Generated by /design-tests on 2026-09-06**
**Scope:** Diver Boy's real Grapple Intercept rock burst, specifically the sphere spacing and one-response collision contract Marc described.

## What this file does

It builds the same `GrappleInterceptMinigame` that a special battle launches, with a live `SubViewport`, `Camera3D`, and `Diver`. It starts the burst and drives the public automatic aim hook until the encounter ends.

## Public interface

| Symbol | Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `GrappleInterceptMinigame.run()` | minigame lifecycle | Creates the production five-rock burst. |
| `GrappleInterceptMinigame.TARGET_COUNT` | content contract | Number of simultaneous rocks a player must resolve. |
| `GrappleInterceptMinigame.auto_intercept_closest()` | supported verification hook | Resolves the actual active weak spot through production hit selection. |
| `finished` / `object_hit` | outcome signals | Observable win/loss effects. |

## Load-bearing comments

- The burst deliberately uses five different grid squares; that only works if a square is large enough for a rock.
- Rocks are described as a visible incoming group, not a stack of overlapping meshes.
- The intended player cost is a rock landing, not a collision bug before the player can react.

## IO boundaries and branching points

- Frame time / tween motion moves the rocks.
- `positions.shuffle()` randomizes which five of eight grid cells launch.
- `_assign_next_weak_spot()` chooses a live target randomly.
- `_shoot()` branches between miss and weak-spot hit; `_land()` branches between an active and non-active weak-spot rock.

## Existing coverage

- The pre-existing test proves automated aim can finish the encounter with no impacts.
- It did not inspect the initial real burst, so it could pass while five rock meshes were already intersecting before the player got control.

| # | Bug | Blast radius | Plausibility | Test type | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 2 | Two spheres collide while approaching but receive more than one impulse before separating. | High — makes the vortex stutter or reverse twice. | A per-frame overlap response can process a separating contact again. | motion invariant/property + live scene | characterized |

## Test plan

### Bug #1 — overlapping launch burst

- **Test type:** live-scene invariant.
- **Description string:** `GRAPPLE INTERCEPT: burst spheres start separated — guards against overlap-driven double bounces`.
- **What it catches:** any shuffled five-rock burst containing a pair closer than their two visible radii.
- **Self-critique:** it observes the constructed production minigame after its normal title hold, not a layout constant or private grid calculation. It survives any refactor that preserves physically separate launch spheres.

### Bug #2 — duplicate impulse on a separating pair

- **Test type:** motion invariant.
- **Description string:** `GRAPPLE COLLISION: separating spheres receive no second impulse — guards against double bounce`.
- **What it catches:** a resolver that fires again after its first elastic response.
- **Self-critique:** it will assert positions and velocities at the collision boundary rather than Tween/loop implementation details.

## Skipped

- Pixel-level vortex appearance: camera framing and art can evolve; separation and one impulse are the stable physical contract.
- Godot `SphereCast3D`: these rocks are manually animated meshes, not physics bodies. Testing a different physics API would not prove the player-facing motion.
- All random five-of-eight combinations: the first live invariant catches any chosen overlapping pair now; a property test will cover collision normals once the resolver exists.

## Post-write evaluation

- **Bugs caught:** #1. The untouched PR burst had four overlapping pairs on its first live run.
- **Bugs characterized:** #2 across eight axis/diagonal contact normals and the real five-rock movement loop after trajectories reach contact distance, plus #3 by the existing completion test.
- **Bugs discovered during writing:** the original sphere Tweens were a second, competing transform writer; even spacing-only repair could not produce a reliable bounce because the next Tween frame would restore the pre-collision trajectory.
